title: Umqombothi
author: Gogo Nomvula
desc: Sorghum malt and maize meal soured overnight, boiled thick, then fermented three days in a bucket with more malt — the home-brewed beer poured at weddings, funerals and ceremonies for the ancestors.
longDesc: Umqombothi is not a craft project. It is the beer brewed for the occasions that matter — umembeso, funerals, the rituals where the ancestors are addressed — and in many households it is still made by the women of the family rather than bought. The process takes three days and produces ten litres of a thick, sour, low-alcohol beer that is drunk from a shared clay vessel and passed. It is gritty and it is meant to be.
ingredients: 1 kg sorghum malt — King Korn Mtombo or equivalent
// Optional, to help the ferment along
2 L shop-bought sorghum beer, added on the second day
equipment: Large food-grade plastic bucket with a cover
steps: Mix half the sorghum malt with the maize meal. Add 2 litres of boiling water and stir to a smooth paste.
Let it cool, cover with a lid, and leave it somewhere warm overnight to begin souring.
The next day, boil 4 litres of the remaining water in a large pot, take it off the heat, and work the soured mixture in, stirring constantly.
Return it to the heat and cook, stirring constantly, until it comes to the boil. It will want to catch, so do not stop stirring.
Cook for 60 minutes, until thick. Cool, then transfer to a large plastic bucket.

Add the remaining 6 litres of cold water, the rest of the sorghum malt and the brown sugar. Cover and set aside for 2 to 3 days to ferment. On the second day you can stir in the shop-bought sorghum beer to help it along.
By the third day it should smell pungent and carry tiny bubbles across the surface.
Press it through a large fine-mesh sieve, by hand or with a wooden spoon, until you have a smooth liquid.
Let it settle for 30 minutes before serving.
chefTips: Stir constantly through the cooking stage. A thick maize-and-malt mixture catches on the base of the pot in seconds and burnt umqombothi cannot be saved.
Judge readiness by smell and by the bubbles on the surface, not by the calendar. A warm kitchen ferments faster than a cold one.
Two litres of commercial sorghum beer on the second day is a widely used shortcut when the ferment looks sluggish.
Use a food-grade bucket with a cover, not a sealed lid. The ferment needs to breathe.
The grit is not a fault. Sieving takes out the coarse solids but umqombothi is meant to have body.
commonMistakes: Walking away during the boil, which scorches the base and taints the whole batch.
Sieving too early, before the pungent smell and surface bubbles appear.
Serving it straight from the sieve without the 30-minute settle, so the first cup is all sediment.
storage: Refrigerate and drink within 2 to 3 days. It continues fermenting and grows sharper.
reheating: Never heated — served cool or at room temperature.
healthBenefits: Low in alcohol compared with commercial beer, typically around 3 per cent.
Fermented sorghum carries B vitamins and live cultures.
Sorghum is gluten-free, though the maize meal is processed alongside other grains in most mills.
culturalNote: Umqombothi is poured at ceremonies where the ancestors are addressed, and the brewing is itself part of the occasion rather than preparation for it. It is distinct from the commercial sorghum beers sold in cartons, which some households will use to help a slow ferment but nobody confuses with the real thing.
